name: Septoria-type Leaf Spot
why: Small circular leaf spots can develop pale centers with tiny dark structures; many other leaf spots look similar.
action: Check lower leaves, reduce splashing and seek host-specific confirmation.

name: Anthracnose-type Damage
why: Sunken lesions on fruit or stems and irregular leaf lesions may fit anthracnose on susceptible hosts.
action: Avoid handling wet plants, remove affected fruit and verify the host and pathogen.

name: Botrytis / Gray Mold-type Symptoms
why: Gray fuzzy growth on dying flowers or rotting tissue may indicate Botrytis.
action: Remove dead flowers, reduce humidity and improve air circulation before considering crop-specific treatment.

name: Damping-off of Seedlings
why: Seedlings collapsing at a narrowed or rotted soil line suggest damping-off or another seedling injury.
action: Use clean containers and fresh seed-starting media; reduce saturation and improve airflow.

name: Blossom-end Rot-type Injury
why: A dark sunken patch at the blossom end may reflect a localized calcium-transport problem, not a contagious rot.
action: Stabilize soil moisture and use soil-test guidance; adding calcium without evidence may not help.

name: Blossom Drop / Pollination Stress
why: Flower loss or young fruit failing to develop can follow temperature stress or incomplete pollination.
action: Check the crop's temperature range, flowering pattern and pollinator access before treating for disease.

name: Fruit Cracking
why: Rapid changes in water supply can split expanding fruit.
action: Maintain steadier soil moisture and harvest ripe fruit promptly; discard fruit with decay.

name: Edema / Corky Blisters
why: Blisters that become corky can occur when water uptake exceeds leaf water loss.
action: Check the leaf underside, improve ventilation and adjust watering; confirm before using a pesticide.

name: Possible Fertilizer / Salt Injury
why: Leaf-edge scorch with salt crust or recent heavy fertilizer may indicate soluble-salt stress.
action: Review fertilizer rates and water quality; test soil or container media before corrective treatment.

name: Possible Herbicide Injury
why: Distorted new growth after nearby spraying can suggest herbicide exposure, though viruses and pests can look similar.
action: Record timing and products used nearby, avoid additional stress and seek Extension assessment.

name: Transplant Shock / Root Disturbance
why: Recently moved plants may wilt or pause growth while roots re-establish.
action: Check root-zone moisture, avoid overfertilizing and provide temporary protection suited to the crop.

name: Vascular Wilt-type Symptoms
why: One-sided wilt and discolored internal stem tissue can occur with vascular wilt pathogens and other injuries.
action: Confirm with a diagnostic service; rotation and resistant varieties depend on the identified cause.

name: Mosaic / Virus-like Symptoms
why: Mottled light-and-dark patterns with distortion may indicate a virus, nutrient injury or chemical damage.
action: Inspect for vectors, avoid moving suspect propagation material and obtain confirmation.

name: Fire Blight-type Symptoms
why: Darkened shoots curled at their tips can fit fire blight on susceptible rose-family hosts such as apple and pear.
action: Check the host first and ask Extension about pruning timing; avoid cutting wet infected growth.

name: Tomato Leaf Mold-type Symptoms
why: Yellow patches above olive-brown growth beneath tomato leaves can indicate leaf mold.
action: Improve ventilation, reduce sustained humidity and confirm before treatment.

name: Rose Black Spot-type Symptoms
why: Black fringed spots and yellowing on roses may indicate black spot.
action: Remove fallen infected leaves, water at soil level and choose resistant varieties where practical.

name: Clubroot-type Symptoms
why: Club-like root swellings on brassicas can fit clubroot, but root-knot nematodes and other problems differ.
action: Confirm the cause before changing pH or moving soil; rotation and sanitation need host-specific guidance.

name: Sooty Mold on Honeydew
why: A dark surface coating on sticky foliage often grows on honeydew from sap-feeding insects.
action: Inspect for scale, aphids or whiteflies; address the insect source instead of treating the coating alone.

name: Japanese Beetles
why: Metallic green-and-copper beetles can skeletonize leaves and feed on flowers.
action: Confirm the beetle and hand-pick small numbers; avoid traps beside susceptible plants.

name: Flea Beetles
why: Tiny jumping beetles and many small holes can be characteristic.
action: Protect vulnerable young crops with suitable covers and check crop-specific thresholds.

name: Cucumber Beetles
why: Striped or spotted beetles on cucurbits can feed and may spread bacterial wilt.
action: Identify the beetle, scout young plants and remove covers when pollination is needed.

name: Squash Bugs
why: Bronze egg clusters and flat gray squash bugs can occur beneath cucurbit leaves.
action: Inspect leaf undersides, remove eggs and use crop-appropriate integrated management.

name: Squash Vine Borer
why: A wilted squash vine with a hole and moist frass near its base may contain a borer.
action: Inspect the stem base, confirm the larva and plan prevention before larvae enter stems.

name: Leafminers
why: Pale winding tunnels or blotches within a leaf can indicate mining larvae.
action: Confirm active mines and the host; remove limited affected leaves when appropriate and avoid harming natural enemies.

name: Mealybugs
why: White cottony insects often gather at leaf joints and protected stems.
action: Isolate affected container plants, inspect crevices and verify species before choosing controls.

name: Stink Bugs / Fruit-feeding Bugs
why: Shield-shaped bugs and pale corky spots on fruit may indicate feeding injury.
action: Confirm the insect because predatory bugs can look similar; scout and use exclusion where suitable.

name: Cutworms
why: Young stems cut near the soil line can indicate nocturnal cutworm feeding.
action: Inspect soil around fresh damage after dusk and consider seedling collars.

name: Leafhoppers
why: Small wedge-shaped jumping insects may cause stippling or leaf-edge hopperburn.
action: Confirm the insect and host; drought and mites can cause similar injury.

name: Colorado Potato Beetles
why: Yellow-and-black striped rounded adults or orange-red larvae can defoliate solanaceous crops.
action: Inspect leaf undersides for eggs, hand-remove small populations and rotate crop locations.

name: Possible Root-knot Nematodes
why: Root galls with poor growth may suggest root-knot nematodes; legume nodules and other swellings differ.
action: Use a diagnostic soil/root sample to confirm before deciding on resistant crops or rotation.

name: Earwig Feeding — Confirm First
why: Pincer-tailed earwigs may chew tender tissue, but also consume other insects and decaying material.
action: Inspect after dark and confirm active feeding before controlling a potentially helpful insect.
